newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD - Australian markets focus on jobs.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD - Australian markets focus on jobs.

text.p: Employment data should dominate Australian markets this week, with last Friday's strong U.S. non-farm payrolls figures setting the early tone before local data for December, due on Thursday, moves to centre stage.
The labour market was one of the weakest areas of the Australian economy in 1996, and a key factor behind the three interest rate cuts in the second half of the year.
The picture is not expected to change much in December.
A small rise of 5,000 is expected, but economists said that following two months of strong growth, the risks to forecasts were on the downside.
Ahead of the labour force data, housing finance for November will be released on Tuesday.
Although the median forecast for the data is for a small rise, Australian Bankers Association data released late on Friday was suggesting a small fall in the month.
November's 50 basis point interest rate cut is expected to have minimal impact on the data.
However, in coming months the combined impact of the November and December cuts, which reduced official interest rates to 6.0 percent, is expected to be reflected in some stronger data.
Westpac's consumer sentiment survey for January will be released on Wednesday.
The last consumer sentiment reading was compiled ahead of the December 11 rate cut, and showed a sizeable fall.
While the rate cut was positive for sentiment, it may be overshadowed in consumers' minds by last week's news of a widening current account deficit and weak retail sales.
BONDS (Fri 10-yr cash 7.51 pct, 3-yr cash 6.65)
Australian bonds will start the week under pressure after U.S. Treasuries ended lower on Friday following stronger than expected December jobs growth.
U.S. payrolls expanded by 262,000 jobs, more than forecast.
Expectations of a reasonably flat local labour force report on Thursday, fuelling last week's speculation of a further easing in monetary policy, could see the market outperform the U.S. this week.

Anticipation of a benign quarterly inflation report later this month could also help the Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread to tighten having broken back below 100 basis points last week, analysts said.

"One only has to consider that Australia's annual underlying inflation will be around one percentrage point below U.S. core CPI, but 10-year yields around one percentage point higher, to see the relative value if the long end of the Australian yield curve," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank.
"The spread could fall to 75 basis points or below over the next few weeks," he added.
This spread briefly touched the low 80s after the Reserve Bank last cut official interest rates to 6.0 percent on December 11, its lowest differential in some 2-1/2 years.
There was also some talk that the Australian Treasury would resume its bond funding programme next week, having last offered fixed rate stock to the market on December 10.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri close US$0.7758/63, NY $US0.7818/25)

The Australian dollar faces an uncertain future after tumbling 1-1/2 cents last week to a five month low and breaching no less than three major technical levels in the process at US$0.7850, US$0.7810 and US$0.7765.
Chart watchers were uniformly bearish and looked for a test of US$0.7720 with a real risk of re-visiting the August 3 trough of US$0.7680 in the short term.
Fundamentals had also turned negative as the Tokyo stock market went into free fall losing 10 percent in a week.
At first the fall was seen as dollar positive since it promised to keep Japanese interest rates at record lows for months to come, and so safeguard the dollar's yield premium.
Now, however, the Nikkei looked in danger of meltdown which threatened to deepen the bad loan situation amongst Japanese financial instituions and derail the fragile economic recovery.

Since Japan was the single largest buyer of Australian exports, that scenario had grave implications for the current account deficit and ultimately the dollar. A slowdown in the Japanese economy would also make it hard for commodity prices to make the gains many A$ supporters had been hoping for this year.

Talk of another RBA rate cut had also gathered adherents and dealers feared a weak employment report Thursday would stoke the speculation to fever pitch, furthering endangering the dollar's attraction to offshore investors.
AUSTRALIAN SHARES (Friday All Ords 2,418.6, down 4.6)
Australian shares are seen starting the week on a positive note after Wall Street overcame stiff early selling on Friday to add 78 points and set a new record close of 6,703.67.
Dealers said the volatile U.S. market was likely to remain the key focus for local investors for the rest of January.
"January is usually the most volatile month for the Australian market because of a lack of corporate information and generally thinner than usual trade," one Brisbane dealer said.
The All Ordinaries index added a modest 19.1 points last week and touched a record intra-day high of 2,348.8 on Friday before pulling back ahead of the release of U.S. jobs data.
The monthly employment figures were higher than expected, putting U.S. bonds into a tailspin.
U.S. stocks initially followed bonds down, but reversed course as investors seized on some of the brighter implications of a stronger than expected economy.

Dealers said the resource sector was likely to remain favoured over industrials with expectations of a worldwide pickup in demand for metals and minerals continuing to underpin support for the major miners.
Corporate events of note include a general meeting of Advance Bank of Australia Ltd shareholders in Sydney on Monday to approve changes to its articles of association.
This meeting is effectively the last hurdle Advance needs to clear before its shareholders can reap the benefits of its planned merger with St George Bank Ltd.

Investors nervously await the first half sales figures from major retailer Woolworths Ltd which are expected to be released on Tuesday and will give a further indication of how Australia's retailers fared over the Christmas period.
The most important scheduled event for the week is on Wednesday when Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd holds its annual meeting in Melbourne.

Dealers said the most significant piece of economic data out next week, Thursday's labour force report, was unlikely to have much influence on the share market, although share investors would keep an eye on the local bond market if the figures are well outside expecations.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
